questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: The rank of \((m \times n)\) matrix \((m < n)\) cannot be more than
questions.explanation:
We know that: \[\rho(A_{m \times n}) \leq \min \{m, n\}\] Given the condition that \(m < n\): \[\min \{m, n\} = m\] \[\rho(A_{m \times n}) \leq m\] Hence, the rank of an \(m \times n\) matrix where \(m < n\) cannot be more than \(m\). \[\boxed{\text{(A) m}}\]
Key points
  • Rank Property: The rank of a matrix is the maximum number of linearly independent row or column vectors.
  • Order Constraint: For \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), \(\text{rank}(A) \leq \min(m, n)\).

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: The following system of equations \[x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 3\] \[x_1 - x_3 = 0\] \[x_1 - x_2 + x_3 = 1\] has
questions.explanation: Given the system of linear equations \(AX = B\): \[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\] \[[A|B] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & \big| & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 & \big| & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 & \big| & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] Applying \(R_{2} \rightarrow R_{2} - R_{1}\) and \(R_{3} \rightarrow R_{3} - R_{1}\): \[[A|B] \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & \big| & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & \big| & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & \big| & -2 \end{bmatrix}\] Applying \(R_{3} \rightarrow R_{3} - 2R_{2}\): \[[A|B] \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & \big| & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & \big| & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & \big| & 4 \end{bmatrix}\] From the row-echelon form, \(\rho(A) = \rho(A|B) = n = 3\), the system is consistent and has a unique solution. \[\boxed{\text{(A) Unique solution}}\]

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question:
Match each of the items A, B and C with an appropriate item from 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.
  1. (A) \(a_1 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + a_2\,y \dfrac{dy}{dx} + a_3\, y = a_4\)
  2. (B) \(a_1 \dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3} + a_2\, y = a_3\)
  3. (C) \(a_1 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} + a_2\, x \dfrac{dy}{dx} + a_3\, x^2 y = 0\)
  1. Non-linear differential equation
  2. Linear differential equation with constant coefficient
  3. Linear homogeneous differential equation
  4. Non-linear homogeneous differential equation
  5. Non-linear first order differential equation
questions.explanation:
Given the classifications: \[\begin{array}{ll} 1. & \text{Non-linear differential equation} \\ 2. & \text{Linear differential equation with constant coefficients} \\ 3. & \text{Linear homogeneous differential equation} \\ 4. & \text{Non-linear homogeneous differential equation} \\ 5. & \text{Non-linear first-order differential equation} \end{array}\] We classify each equation individually. For (A), \[a_1\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + a_2\,y\frac{dy}{dx} + a_3y = a_4\] The term \(y\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) contains a product of the dependent variable and its derivative. Hence, this is a Non-linear differential equation. For (B), \[a_1\frac{d^3y}{dx^3} + a_2y = a_3\] All derivatives appear to the first power and are not multiplied together. Also, \(a_1,a_2,a_3\) are constants. Therefore, it is a Linear differential equation with constant coefficients. For (C), \[a_1\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + a_2\,x\frac{dy}{dx} + a_3x^2y = 0\] The equation is sometimes incorrectly grouped with "non-linear" types due to coefficients involve the independent variable (\(x\)) raised to powers (like \(x^2\)). Because it does not possess constant coefficients. Also, the right-hand side is zero. Therefore, it is a Non-linear homogeneous differential equation. Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{(A) A--1, B--2, C--4}}\]
Key points
  • A differential equation is linear if the dependent variable and all its derivatives appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together.
  • Constant coefficients imply that the coefficients of \(y\) and its derivatives are constants.

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: A ramp voltage, \(v(t) = 100\,t\text{ Volts}\), is applied to an \(RC\) differentiating circuit with \(R = 5\ \text{k}\Omega\) and \(C = 4\ \mu\text{F}\). The maximum output voltage is
questions.explanation: For an RC differentiating circuit, \[V_o = RC\frac{dv_i}{dt}\] Given, \(v_i(t)=100t\) Hence, \[\frac{dv_i}{dt} = 100~\text{V/s}\] Therefore, \[V_o = (5\times10^3)(4\times10^{-6})(100) = 2~\text{V}\] Since the slope of the ramp input is constant, the output voltage is constant. Hence, the maximum output voltage is \[\boxed{2~\text{V}}\] Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }2.0~\text{V}}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.ref: 2nd Order Dynamics and Complex Impedance Q1
questions.question: \(Z(s) = \dfrac{5}{s^2+4}\) represents the input impedance of a network. (Mention True or False.)
questions.explanation: A driving-point function (such as an input impedance \(Z(s)\) or input admittance \(Y(s)\)) of a passive network must be physically realizable using actual passive components (\(R\), \(L\), and \(C\)). Thus the degrees of the numerator and denominator polynomials cannot differ by more than \(1\). The mathematical and physical reasons for this constraint are detailed below: 1. High-Frequency Behavior (\(s \to \infty\)) At extremely high frequencies, any physically realizable passive network must simplify to look like either a single resistor, a single inductor, or a single capacitor. Let \(n\) be the highest degree of the numerator polynomial \(N(s)\), and \(m\) be the highest degree of the denominator polynomial \(D(s)\). As \(s \to \infty\), the behavior of \(Z(s)\) is dominated by its highest-order terms: \[Z(s) \approx H \cdot s^{(n-m)}\] Depending on the difference between \(n\) and \(m\), three physical cases can exist for a passive element: Case 1 (\(n - m = 1\)): \(Z(s) \approx H \cdot s\), which represents a pure inductor (\(Z(s) = sL\)). Case 2 (\(n - m = 0\)): \(Z(s) \approx H\), which represents a pure resistor (\(Z(s) = R\)). Case 3 (\(m - n = 1\)): \(Z(s) \approx \frac{H}{s}\), which represents a pure capacitor (\(Z(s) = \frac{1}{sC}\)). For the given input impedance function: \[Z(s) = \frac{5}{s^2 + 4}\] Here, \(n = 0\) and \(m = 2\). The degree difference is \(m - n = 2\). As \(s \to \infty\): \[Z(s) \approx \frac{5}{s^2}\] There is no individual passive component or combination of components whose basic impedance decreases proportionally to \(\frac{1}{s^2}\) at high frequencies. 2. Multiplicity of Poles at Infinity For a network function to be realizable, any poles or zeros located on the imaginary axis (\(j\omega\)-axis), including the point at infinity, must be simple (i.e., they must have a multiplicity/order of exactly \(1\)). If we examine the corresponding admittance function \(Y(s)\): \[Y(s) = \frac{1}{Z(s)} = \frac{s^2 + 4}{5} = \frac{1}{5}s^2 + \frac{4}{5}\] Taking the limit as \(s \to \infty\), the admittance becomes: \[\lim_{s \to \infty} Y(s) \propto s^2\] This indicates that \(Y(s)\) has a pole at infinity of order 2. Therefore, because the difference in degrees is \(2\), the function cannot represent the input impedance of a passive network. \[\boxed{\text{False}}\]

questions.question: A series RLC circuit consisting of \(R = 10\Omega\), \(|X_L|=20\Omega\) and \(|X_C|= 20\Omega\), is connected across an a.c. supply of 200 V rms. The rms voltage across the capacitor is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
From the given data capacitive impedance \(X_C=-j20\Omega\) and inductive reactance \(X_L=j20\Omega\). Since it is a series RLC circuit and \(X_L=-X_C\), the circuit is at resonance. \[V_R=200V_{rms}\] Hence \(V_C=-jQV_R\) Here \(Q=|X_L|/R=20/10=2\) \[\therefore, V_C=-j2\times200V_{rms}=400\angle-90^{\circ}V_{rms}\]
Method 2
From the given data capacitive impedance \(X_C=-j20\Omega\) and inductive reactance \(X_L=j20\Omega\). Since it is a series RLC circuit and \(X)L=-X_C\), the circuit is at resonance, and the circuit impedance equals the resistance. \[V_R=200V_{rms}\] \[I = 200/10 = 20A\]= Thus \(V_C = IX_C\) \[V_C=20\times -j20=-j400 V_{rms}=400\angle-90^{\circ}V_{rms}\]
\[\boxed{(d) 400\angle-90^{\circ}}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Match each of the items A, B and C with an appropriate item from 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. (A) \(a_1 \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} + a_2 y \frac{dy}{dx} + a_3 y = a_4\) (B) \(a_1 \frac{d^3 y}{dx^3} + a_2 y = a_3\) (C) \(a_1 \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} + a_2 x \frac{dy}{dx} + a_3 x^2 y = 0\) (1) Non-liner differential equation (2) Linear differential equation with constant coefficients (3) Linear homogeneous differential equation (4) Non-linear homogeneous differential equation (5) Non-linear first order differential equation
questions.explanation:
Let's analyze each given differential equation to determine its type. Equation (A):
\[a_{1} \frac{d^{2} y}{dx^{2}} + a_{2} y \frac{dy}{dx} + a_{3} y = a_{4}\] The presence of the term \(a_{2} y \frac{dy}{dx}\) involves the product of the dependent variable \(y\) and its derivative \(\frac{dy}{dx}\). This property makes the differential equation non-linear. Thus, (A) matches with (1) Non-linear differential equation. Equation (B):
\[a_{1} \frac{d^{3} y}{dx^{3}} + a_{2} y = a_{3}\] The dependent variable \(y\) and its derivatives appear only with a degree of 1, and there are no cross-products between them. Assuming \(a_{1}\), \(a_{2}\), and \(a_{3}\) are constants, this represents a linear equation with constant coefficients. Thus, (B) matches with (2) Linear differential equation with constant coefficients. Equation (C):
\[a_{1} \frac{d^{2} y}{dx^{2}} + a_{2} x \frac{dy}{dx} + a_{3} x^{2} y = 0\] This equation is linear because \(y\) and its derivatives are of the first degree. The right-hand side is equal to \(0\), which signifies that the equation is homogeneous. Although the coefficients are functions of \(x\), it satisfies the condition of being linear and homogeneous. Thus, (C) matches with (3) Linear homogeneous differential equation. \[\boxed{\text{A} \rightarrow 1, \text{B} \rightarrow 2, \text{C} \rightarrow 3}\]
Key points
  • A differential equation is linear if the dependent variable and all its derivatives appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together.
  • A differential equation is non-linear if it contains products of the dependent variable and its derivatives (e.g., \(y \frac{dy}{dx}\)), or if the dependent variable/derivatives are raised to a power other than 1.
  • A linear differential equation is homogeneous if the term independent of the dependent variable and its derivatives is zero (i.e., the RHS is 0).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The Fourier Series of a odd periodic function, contains only
questions.explanation: A periodic function \(f(t)\) is classified as an odd function if it satisfies the condition \(f(t) = -f(-t)\). The trigonometric Fourier series of a periodic function is given by: \[f(t) = a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left[ a_n \cos(n\omega_0 t) + b_n \sin(n\omega_0 t) \right]\] The Fourier coefficients are evaluated over a symmetric period \(T_0\) as follows: 1. DC Component (\(a_0\)): \[a_0 = \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{-T_0/2}^{T_0/2} f(t) \, dt\] Since \(f(t)\) is an odd function, its integral over a symmetrical interval \([-T_0/2, T_0/2]\) evaluates to zero. Thus, \(a_0 = 0\). 2. Cosine Coefficients (\(a_n\)): \[a_n = \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{-T_0/2}^{T_0/2} f(t) \cos(n\omega_0 t) \, dt\] The product of an odd function \(f(t)\) and an even function \(\cos(n\omega_0 t)\) yields an odd function. Integrating this odd function over a symmetrical interval results in zero. Thus, \(a_n = 0\). 3. Sine Coefficients (\(b_n\)): \[b_n = \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{-T_0/2}^{T_0/2} f(t) \sin(n\omega_0 t) \, dt\] The product of an odd function \(f(t)\) and another odd function \(\sin(n\omega_0 t)\) yields an even function. The integral of an even function over a symmetric interval is generally non-zero. \[\implies b_n \neq 0\] Therefore, the Fourier series of an odd periodic function contains only sine terms. \[\boxed{\text{D) sine terms }}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Increased pulse-width in the flat-top sampling, leads to
options: attenuation of high frequencies in reproduction
attenuation of low frequencies in reproduction
questions.explanation:
In flat-top sampling, the sampled signal can be modeled as the convolution of an ideally sampled impulse train with a rectangular pulse \(p(t)\) of duration \(\tau\) (the pulse-width). In the frequency domain, this operation corresponds to multiplying the periodically repeated spectrum of the message signal by the Fourier transform of the rectangular pulse, which is a sinc function: \[P(f) = \tau \text{sinc}(f\tau)\] Because the magnitude of the sinc function decreases as the frequency \(f\) increases, it acts as a low-pass filter, attenuating the higher frequency components of the original message spectrum \(M(f)\). This phenomenon is known as the aperture effect. If the pulse-width \(\tau\) is increased, the sinc function \(P(f)\) narrows in the frequency domain (its first zero-crossing at \(1/\tau\) moves closer to the origin). This results in a steeper roll-off within the baseband bandwidth \(W\), leading to greater attenuation of the high-frequency components in the reproduced signal. \[\boxed{\text{A) attenuation of high frequencies in reproduction }}\]
Key points
  • Aperture Effect: The amplitude distortion in flat-top sampling caused by the finite width of the sampling pulses.
  • Larger pulse-width \(\implies\) narrower sinc envelope \(\implies\) more severe high-frequency attenuation.
  • To correct this distortion during demodulation, an equalizer filter with a magnitude response inversely proportional to the sinc function is placed before the reconstruction low-pass filter.

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The laplace transform of a unit ramp function starting at t=a, is
questions.explanation:
A unit ramp function starting at time \(t = a\) can be mathematically represented as: \[f(t) = (t-a)u(t-a)\] We know the standard Laplace transform of a basic unit ramp function \(r(t) = tu(t)\) is: \[\mathcal{L}\{tu(t)\} = \frac{1}{s^2}\] Using the time-shifting property of the Laplace transform, which states that if \(\mathcal{L}\{x(t)\} = X(s)\), then for a delayed function: \[\mathcal{L}\{x(t-a)u(t-a)\} = e^{-as}X(s)\] Applying this property to our ramp function with a delay of \(a\): \[\mathcal{L}\{(t-a)u(t-a)\} = e^{-as} \left(\frac{1}{s^2}\right) = \frac{e^{-as}}{s^2}\] \[\boxed{\text{C) }\frac{e^{-as}}{s^2}}\]
Key points
  • The Laplace transform of a standard unit ramp function \(r(t) = tu(t)\) is \(\frac{1}{s^2}\).
  • Time-Shifting Theorem: A shift (delay) of \(a\) units in the time domain results in multiplication by \(e^{-as}\) in the Laplace domain.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question:
Match the following: List-I:
  1. A. The current gain of a BJT will be increased.
  2. B. The current gain of a BJT will be reduced.
  3. C. The break-down voltage of a BJT will be reduced.
List-II:
  1. The collector doping concentration is increased.
  2. The base width is reduced.
  3. The emitter doping concentration to base doping concentration ratio is reduced.
  4. The base doping concentration is increased keeping the ratio of the emitter doping concentration to base doping concentration constant.
  5. The collector doping concentration is reduced.
questions.explanation:
• A - 2: As the base width of the BJT is reduced, the recombination current (base current \(I_B\)) decreases. As a result collector current (\(I_C\)) increases and consequently, the current gain \(\alpha=\dfrac{I_C}{I_E}=\dfrac{I_C}{I_C+I_B}\) of the BJT increases.
  • B - 3: If the emitter doping concentration to base doping concentration ratio is reduced then the emitter injection efficiency \(\gamma\) decreases, so the current gain \(\alpha\) of BJT reduces.
  • C - 1: If the collector doping concentration is increased then the breakdown voltage (\(V_{BR}\)) of a BJT will be reduced.
\[\boxed{A-2\,, \, B-3\,,\, C-1}\]
Key points
  • The emitter injection efficiency for a PNP transistor is given as: \[\gamma =\frac{{{I_{pE}}}}{{{I_{pE}} + {I_{n E}}}}\]
  • In terms of device parameters , emitter injection efficiency is given by: \[\gamma =\frac{1}{1+ \dfrac{D_E N_B x_B}{D_B N_E x_E}}\] Where \(N_E\) and \(N_B\) are the emitter and base doping concentrations, \(D_E\) and \(D_B\) are diffusion coefficients, and \(x_E\) and \(x_B\) are the space charge region widths.
  • The relation between \(\gamma\) and \(\alpha\) is given as \(\alpha=\gamma b\), where \(b\) is the base transport factor.

questions.question: The threshold voltage of an n-channel MOSFET can be increased by
questions.explanation: The threshold voltage including the body effect is given by: \[V_T = V_{T_0} + \gamma\left(\sqrt{|-2\phi_F + V_{SB}|} - \sqrt{|2\phi_F|}\right)\] where \(\gamma\) is the substrate bias coefficient and \(V_{SB}\) is the source-to-body voltage, and is defined as: \[\gamma = \frac{\sqrt{2qN_A \epsilon_S}}{C_{ox}} = \frac{ t_{ox} }{\epsilon_{ox}}\sqrt{2qN_A \epsilon_S}\] \(N_A\) is the substrate doping concentration. Increase in \(N_A\) causes decrease in channel carrier concentration and increase in \(V_T\). \[\boxed{(B)\text{ reducing the channel carrier concentration.}}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q1
questions.question: The output of a logic gate is '1' when all its input are at logic '0'.Then gate is either
options: a NAND or an EX-OR gate
a NOR or an EX-NOR gate
an OR or an EX-NOR gate
an AND or an EX-OR gate
questions.explanation:
For all inputs equal to logic \(0\), \[\text{NOR}=\overline{0+0+\cdots}=1\] Also, an EX-NOR gate gives output \(1\) when all its inputs are equal. Hence, \[\text{EX-NOR}(0,0,\ldots,0)=1\] Checking the remaining gates: \[\text{AND}=0,\qquad
\text{OR}=0,\qquad
\text{NAND}=1,\qquad
\text{EX-OR}=0\] Among the given options, only the pair NOR or EX-NOR satisfies the condition. \[\boxed{\text{(b) NOR or an EX-NOR gate}}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: State whether the following statement is True or False: The look-ahead carry adder is a parallel carry adder where all sum digits are generated directly from the input digits.
questions.explanation:
To evaluate the validity of the statement regarding the look-ahead carry adder, we analyze its parallel carry generation equations. A Look-Ahead Carry (LAC) Adder speeds up addition by eliminating sequential propagation delay. From the provided diagram, each stage \(i\) defines:
  • Carry Propagate (\(p_i\)): \(p_i = A_i \oplus B_i\)
  • Carry Generate (\(g_i\)): \(g_i = A_i \cdot B_i\)
Instead of waiting for a carry ripple, the internal carries are evaluated simultaneously in a two-level sum-of-products form using the base input carry \(C_{in}\): \[\begin{aligned} C_1 &= g_0 + p_0 C_{in} \\ C_2 &= g_1 + p_1 g_0 + p_1 p_0 C_{in} \\ C_3 &= g_2 + p_2 g_1 + p_2 p_1 g_0 + p_2 p_1 p_0 C_{in} \\ C_4 &= g_3 + p_3 g_2 + p_3 p_2 g_1 + p_3 p_2 p_1 g_0 + p_3 p_2 p_1 p_0 C_{in} \end{aligned}\] The individual sum bits are then computed concurrently at each stage as \(S_i = p_i \oplus C_i\). Because every single carry and sum expression depends strictly on the initial input digits (\(A_i, B_i, C_{in}\)) via parallel combinational logic, all sum digits are generated simultaneously and directly. Therefore, the statement is \[\boxed{\textbf{True}.}\].
Key points
  • Simultaneous Computation: The central look-ahead logic block produces \(C_1\) through \(C_4\) synchronously, making the total propagation delay constant regardless of bit width.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: A \(2\ \mu\text{sec}\) pulse can be streched into a \(10\text{ m sec}\) pulse by using a ______ circuit.
questions.explanation:
A pulse can be stretched (widened) to a predetermined duration using a monostable multivibrator circuit (also known as a one-shot multivibrator). When triggered by an input pulse of short duration (\(2\,\mu\text{s}\)), the monostable multivibrator enters its quasi-stable state and remains there for a time period determined by its external resistor (\(R\)) and capacitor (\(C\)) components. After this time interval (\(10\,\text{ms}\)), it automatically returns to its stable state, effectively stretching the input pulse. \[\boxed{\text{monostable multivibrator}}\]
Key points
  • Monostable Multivibrator: Has one stable state and one quasi-stable state. It functions as a pulse stretcher or time-delay circuit.
  • Output Pulse Width (\(T\)): Determined by the time constant of the external \(RC\) network (e.g., \(T \approx 1.1 R C\) for a 555 timer in monostable mode).

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: Synchronous counters are ______ than the ripple counters.
questions.explanation:
In synchronous counters, all flip-flops are connected to a common clock signal and trigger simultaneously. Consequently, the propagation delay is equal to the delay of only a single flip-flop plus any combinational logic gating delay. In contrast, ripple (asynchronous) counters pass the clock signal through the flip-flops sequentially in a chain, causing the individual propagation delays to accumulate (\(N \cdot t_{pd}\)). Therefore, synchronous counters operate at much higher speeds. \[\boxed{\text{faster}}\]
Key points
  • Synchronous Counters: Clocked simultaneously; propagation delay does not increase significantly with the number of bits.
  • Ripple Counters: Clocked sequentially; cumulative delay limits the maximum operating frequency.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: A ring oscillator consisting of 5 inverters is runnig at a frequency of \(1.0\text{ MHz}\). The propagation delay per gate is \(\text{n sec}\).
questions.explanation:
The oscillation frequency \(f\) of a ring oscillator consisting of an odd number of inverters \(n\) is given by the formula: \[f = \frac{1}{2 \cdot n \cdot t_{pd}}\] Where:
  • \(n = 5\) is the number of inverters.
  • \(f = 1.0\,\text{MHz} = 1.0 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Hz}\) is the frequency of oscillation.
  • \(t_{pd}\) is the propagation delay per gate.
Rearranging the formula to solve for \(t_{pd}\): \[t_{pd} = \frac{1}{2 \cdot n \cdot f}\] Substituting the given values: \[t_{pd} = \frac{1}{2 \cdot 5 \cdot (1.0 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Hz})}\] \[t_{pd} = \frac{1}{10^{7}}\,\text{s} = 10^{-7}\,\text{s}\] Converting the time delay into nanoseconds (\(\text{ns}\)): \[t_{pd} = 10^{-7} \times 10^{9}\,\text{ns} = 100\,\text{ns}\] \[\boxed{100}\]
Key points
  • Ring Oscillator Frequency: Calculated using \(f = \frac{1}{2n \cdot t_{pd}}\) because a complete wave cycle requires the signal to traverse the entire ring twice (once for the rising edge and once for the falling edge).
  • Condition for Oscillation: The number of inverters \(n\) must be an odd integer to maintain unstable feedback and sustain continuous oscillation.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: Data can be changed from spatial code to temporal code and vice-versa by using
questions.explanation:
• Spatial Code (Parallel Data): Data where all bits are present simultaneously over multiple parallel lines.
  • Temporal Code (Serial Data): Data where bits are arranged sequentially and transmitted one after another over a single line over time.
  • Shift Registers are sequential logic circuits primarily used for parallel-to-serial conversion (spatial to temporal) and serial-to-parallel conversion (temporal to spatial).
\[\boxed{\text{(B) shift-registers}}\]
Key points
  • PISO (Parallel-In Serial-Out) shift registers convert spatial code to temporal code.
  • SIPO (Serial-In Parallel-Out) shift registers convert temporal code to spatial code.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question:
In each of the following questions match each of the items A, B and C with an appropriate option from 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.
Type of ADCMaximum conversion for 8 bit ADC in clock cycles.
(A) Successive approximation(1) 1
(B) Dual-slope(2) 8
(C) Parallel Comparator(3) 16
(4) 256
(5) 512
questions.explanation:
Based on the conversion time characteristics of an \(n\)-bit (\(n = 8\)) Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC):
  • (A) Successive approximation: The conversion requires exactly \(n\) clock cycles regardless of the input voltage. For an 8-bit ADC, the maximum conversion time is \(8\) clock cycles. \(\rightarrow\) (2) 8
  • (B) Dual-slope: The worst-case conversion time occurs when the input voltage is at its maximum value, requiring \(2^{n+1}\) clock cycles. For an 8-bit ADC, this corresponds to \(2^{8+1} = 512\) clock cycles. \(\rightarrow\) (5) 512
  • (C) Parallel Comparator: Also known as a Flash ADC, it processes all bits simultaneously using parallel comparators, taking only a single clock cycle for conversion. \(\rightarrow\) (1) 1
\[\boxed{\text{A-2, B-5, C-1}}\]
Key points
  • Parallel Comparator (Flash) ADC: Conversion time is independent of resolution and equals \(1\) clock cycle.
  • Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC: Conversion time is linearly dependent on resolution, requiring \(n\) clock cycles.
  • Dual-Slope ADC: Slowest conversion speed, requiring a maximum of \(2^{n+1}\) clock cycles.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Families and Semiconductor Memories Q1
questions.question: In the output stage of a standard TTL, have a diode between the emitter of the pull-up transistor and the collector of the pull-down transistor. The purpose of this diode is to isolate the output node from the power supply \(V_{\alpha}\).(True/False)
questions.explanation:
To analyze the statement regarding the output stage of a standard TTL logic gate:
  1. Structure of the TTL Totem-Pole Output Stage:
    The standard TTL output stage (often called the totem-pole configuration) consists of:
    • A pull-up transistor (\(Q_3\)) whose emitter is connected to the anode of a diode (\(D\)).
    • A pull-down transistor (\(Q_4\)) whose collector is connected to the cathode of the diode (\(D\)) and also serves as the output terminal (\(Y\)).
    • The diode (\(D\)) situated between the emitter of the pull-up transistor \(Q_3\) and the collector of the pull-down transistor \(Q_4\).
  2. Actual Purpose of the Diode (\(D\)):
    • When the output is low (logic 0), the phase-splitter transistor (\(Q_2\)) is saturated, forcing the base of the pull-up transistor \(Q_3\) to approximately \(V_{BE4,\text{sat}} + V_{CE2,\text{sat}} \approx 0.7\,\text{V} + 0.2\,\text{V} = 0.9\,\text{V}\).
    • At the same time, the pull-down transistor \(Q_4\) is saturated, pulling the output node (\(Y\)) down to \(V_{CE4,\text{sat}} \approx 0.2\,\text{V}\).
    • Without the diode, the base-to-emitter voltage of \(Q_3\) would be: \[V_{BE3} = V_{B3} - V_Y \approx 0.9\,\text{V} - 0.2\,\text{V} = 0.7\,\text{V}\] This potential is high enough to turn \(Q_3\) partially ON, causing both the pull-up (\(Q_3\)) and pull-down (\(Q_4\)) transistors to conduct simultaneously, leading to heavy current draw from the power supply.
    • Inserting the diode \(D\) adds an extra \(0.7\,\text{V}\) drop in the path. For \(Q_3\) to conduct, the base voltage \(V_{B3}\) must overcome both the \(V_{BE3}\) of the transistor and the forward voltage drop \(V_D\) of the diode: \[V_{B3,\text{req}} = V_Y + V_D + V_{BE3} \approx 0.2\,\text{V} + 0.7\,\text{V} + 0.7\,\text{V} = 1.6\,\text{V}\] Since \(V_{B3}\) is only \(0.9\,\text{V}\), the diode successfully keeps the pull-up transistor \(Q_3\) **completely cut off** when the pull-down transistor \(Q_4\) is ON.
  3. Conclusion:
    The primary purpose of the diode is to keep the pull-up transistor turned off while the pull-down transistor is turned on. It is not to isolate the output node from the power supply \(V_{CC}\) (or \(V_{\alpha}\) in the question text).
Thus, the statement is False. \[\boxed{\text{False}}\]
Key points
  • TTL Totem-Pole Diode: Placed in the output path to prevent simultaneous conduction of both pull-up and pull-down transistors.
  • Off-State Maintenance: The diode shifts the required turn-on voltage of the upper transistor up by approximately \(0.7\,\text{V}\), ensuring it remains reliably in cut-off when the output is low.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Families and Semiconductor Memories Q2
questions.question: A PLA can be used
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct application of a PLA (Programmable Logic Array):
  1. Understanding PLA Structure:
    A PLA is a type of Programmable Logic Device (PLD) consisting of:
    • A programmable AND array (to generate product terms of the inputs).
    • A programmable OR array (to sum the product terms to generate outputs).
  2. Functionality:
    Because it consists strictly of arrays of AND and OR logic gates without any inherent storage/memory elements (like flip-flops or registers) in its standard design, it directly implements sum-of-products boolean functions. Therefore, its primary and fundamental purpose is to realize combinational logic.
  3. Analysis of other options:
    • Option A (as a microprocessor): A microprocessor is a highly complex sequential and control system containing ALUs, registers, and control units; a simple PLA cannot act as a microprocessor.
    • Option B (as a dynamic memory): DRAM is built using capacitors and access transistors to store data charges; a PLA is logic-based and cannot be used as dynamic memory.
    • Option C (to realize sequential logic): Standard PLAs do not contain memory elements (flip-flops). While some registered PLAs (which include flip-flops on the outputs) can realize sequential logic, the standard, fundamental PLA is designed specifically for combinational logic.
\[\boxed{\text{(D) to realise a combinational logic}}\]
Key points
  • PLA Features: Both the AND array and the OR array are programmable, making it highly flexible for implementing combinational sum-of-products expressions.
  • Comparison with PAL/ROM:
    DeviceAND ArrayOR Array
    PROMFixedProgrammable
    PALProgrammableFixed
    PLAProgrammableProgrammable

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Families and Semiconductor Memories Q3
questions.question: A dynamic RAM consists of
questions.explanation:
To determine the basic hardware architecture of a dynamic RAM (DRAM) cell:
  1. Basic Component Design:
    A basic dynamic RAM (DRAM) cell stores a single bit of binary data as an electric charge on a small integrated capacitor. To control the access to this capacitor for reading or writing data, a single MOS transistor is placed in series with it acting as a switch.
  2. The 1T1C Cell Configuration:
    This standard architecture is widely known as the 1T1C cell configuration:
    • 1 Transistor (Access Transistor): The gate of this NMOS/PMOS transistor is connected to the Word Line (WL), while its channel connects the Bit Line (BL) directly to the storage element.
    • 1 Capacitor (Storage Capacitor): Accumulates or releases charge to establish the logical state (1 or 0).
  3. Contrast with Alternative Configurations:
    • 6 Transistors (Option A): Typical structure required to design a standard Static RAM (SRAM) cell utilizing cross-coupled inverters to form a bistable latch.
    • 2 Transistors and 2 Capacitors (Option B) / 2 Capacitors only (Option D): Do not describe the fundamental, elementary layout of modern industrial DRAM arrays.
\[\boxed{\text{(C) 1 transistor and 1 capacitor}}\]
Key points
  • High Packing Density: The simple 1T1C architecture takes up very little silicon area, allowing DRAM to achieve significantly higher data storage capacities per unit chip area compared to SRAM.
  • Volatile Nature & Leaks: Since the charge on the isolated capacitor leaks away naturally over time, dynamic RAM relies on external peripheral circuits to periodically perform a "refresh cycle."

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: Tachometer feedback in a D.C. position control system enhances stability (T/F)
questions.explanation:
Tachometer feedback is a form of derivative feedback. The inclusion of this feedback adds a zero at the origin in the feedback path, which effectively:
  • Increases damping: Reduces oscillations and overshoot.
  • Improves relative stability: Enhances the system's stability margins.
Hence, the statement that tachometer feedback enhances stability is True

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II: List-I
  1. Very low response at very high frequencies
  2. Overshoot
  3. Synchro-control transformer output
List-II
  1. Low Pass systems
  2. Velocity damping
  3. Natural frequency
  4. Phase-sensitive modulation
  5. Damping ratio
questions.explanation:
Based on the characteristics of control systems and components:
  • (a) \(\to\) (1): A system that exhibits a very low response at very high frequencies naturally attenuates high-frequency signals, which is the primary characteristic of a Low Pass system.
  • (b) \(\to\) (5): Maximum overshoot (\(M_{p}\)) in a second-order system is mathematically defined as \(M_{p} = e^{-\left(\frac{\xi\pi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^2}}\right)}\). This clearly shows that overshoot depends directly on the Damping ratio (\(\xi\)).
  • (c) \(\to\) (4): A synchro-control transformer acts as an error detector. Its output is an AC voltage whose magnitude depends on the angular displacement and whose phase depends on the direction of displacement, representing Phase-sensitive modulation.
\[\boxed{a-1, b-5, c-4}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question:
The response of an LCR circuit to a step input is:
  1. Over damped
  2. Critically damped
  3. Oscillatory
If the transfer function has:
  1. poles on the negative real axis
  2. poles on the imaginary axis
  3. multiple poles on the positive real axis
  4. poles on the positive real axis
  5. multiple poles on the negative real axis.
questions.explanation:
The damping behavior of a second-order system, such as an LCR circuit, is determined by the specific location of the roots (poles) of its characteristic polynomial in the \(s\)-plane. By analyzing the transfer function characteristics:
  • Overdamped: When \(\xi > 1\), the poles are real, negative, and distinct, lying on the negative real axis.
  • Critically damped: When \(\xi = 1\), the system has multiple (repeated) poles on the negative real axis.
  • Oscillatory/Undamped: When \(\xi = 0\), the poles are purely imaginary conjugates (\(\pm j\omega_{n}\)), lying on the imaginary axis.
\[\boxed{a-1, b-5, c-2}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: If \(G(s)\) is a stable transfer function, then \(F(s) = \dfrac{1}{G(s)}\) is always a stable transfer function. (T/F).
questions.explanation: Let the transfer function of \(G(s)\) be: \[G(s) = \frac{(s + Z_1)(s + Z_2)}{(s + P_1)(s + P_2)}\] Then the inverted transfer function \(F(s)\) is: \[F(s) = \frac{1}{G(s)} = \frac{(s + P_1)(s + P_2)}{(s + Z_1)(s + Z_2)}\] The condition for the stability of \(G(s)\) is that none of its poles (i.e., \(-P_1, -P_2\)) should lie in the right half of the \(s\)-plane. However, a stable transfer function \(G(s)\) can still have zeros (i.e., \(-Z_1, -Z_2\)) in the right half of the \(s\)-plane (known as a non-minimum phase system). When finding \(F(s) = \dfrac{1}{G(s)}\), these zeros of \(G(s)\) become the poles of \(F(s)\). If any of these zeros lie in the right half of the \(s\)-plane, \(F(s)\) will possess right-half plane poles, making it unstable. Therefore, \(F(s)\) need not always be stable. \[\boxed{\text{False}}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: The bandwidth required for the transmission of a PCM signal increases by a factor of when the number of quantization levels is increased from \(4\) to \(64\).
questions.explanation:
Theory:
In PCM, the transmission bandwidth is proportional to the number of bits per sample. Since the number of bits is \(n=\log_2 L\), increasing the quantization levels increases the required bandwidth. Given, \[L_1 = 4 = 2^2\] \[\Rightarrow n_1 = 2\]and \[L_2 = 64 = 2^6\] \[\Rightarrow n_2 = 6\]The PCM bandwidth is \[(BW)_{\text{PCM}}=\frac{n f_s}{2}\]Therefore, \[\frac{(BW)_2}{(BW)_1} = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{6}{2} = 3\]Hence, the bandwidth increases by a factor of \[\boxed{3}\]

questions.subject: communication-systems
questions.question: A 10 MHz carrier is frequency modulated by a sinusoidal signal of 500Hz, the maximum frequency deviation being 50 kHz. The bandwidth required (in kHz) as given by the Carson’s rule is
questions.explanation:
Theory: Carson's rule estimates the transmission bandwidth of an FM signal using the maximum frequency deviation and the highest modulating frequency. Given,\[f_m=500~\text{Hz},\qquad \Delta f=50~\text{kHz}.\]The modulation index is\[\beta=\frac{\Delta f}{f_m} =\frac{50\times10^3}{500} =100.\]Using Carson's rule,\[BW=2(\beta+1)f_m\] \[=2(100+1)\times500\] \[=101000~\text{Hz}\] \[\boxed{\text{101 kHz}}\]
Key points
  • Carson's rule is \(BW=2(\Delta f+f_m)\).
  • Alternatively, \(BW=2(\beta+1)f_m\).
  • Use the highest modulating frequency in Carson's rule.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use the carrier frequency while calculating FM bandwidth.
  • Do not forget to convert units before substitution.
  • Do not omit the \(+1\) term while using \(BW=2(\beta+1)f_m\).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A plane electromagnetic wave travelling along the \(+z\)-direction, has its electric field given by \(E_x = 2 \cos(\omega t)\) and \(E_y = 2 \cos(\omega t + 90^\circ)\) The wave is
questions.explanation:
Circular polarization occurs when two orthogonal electric field components have equal amplitudes and a phase difference of \(90^\circ\) (or \(\pi/2\) radians). Consider the components: [figure unavailable] \[E_x = 2 \cos(\omega t)\] \[E_y = 2 \cos(\omega t + 90^\circ) = -2 \sin(\omega t)\] To determine the sense of rotation, we trace the vector \(\vec{E} = E_x \hat{a}_x + E_y \hat{a}_y\) over time:
  • At \(t = 0\): \(E_x = 2\), \(E_y = 0 \implies \vec{E} = 2 \hat{a}_x\)
  • At \(t = T/4\) (where \(T = 2\pi/\omega\)): \(E_x = 0\), \(E_y = -2 \implies \vec{E} = -2 \hat{a}_y\)
Tracing these points shows that for a wave propagating in the \(+z\) direction, the tip of the electric field vector rotates clockwise as viewed from the direction of propagation. This defines Left Circular Polarization (LCP). \[\boxed{(C):\text{Left Circular Polarization}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: If a pure resistance load, when connected to a lossless \(75\ \Omega\) line, produces a VSWR of \(3\) on the line, then the load impedance can only be \(25\ \Omega\).
questions.explanation: For a pure resistive load on a lossless transmission line, the Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) is defined as: \[\text{VSWR} = \frac{R_{L}}{R_{0}} \quad \text{if } R_{L} > R_{0}\] \[\text{VSWR} = \frac{R_{0}}{R_{L}} \quad \text{if } R_{0} > R_{L}\] Given \(\text{VSWR} = 3\) and \(R_{0} = 75\,\Omega\), we evaluate both cases to find the possible values for \(R_{L}\). Case 1: \(R_{L} > R_{0}\) \[R_{L} = \text{VSWR} \times R_{0}\] \[R_{L} = 3 \times 75 = 225\,\Omega\] Case 2: \(R_{0} > R_{L}\) \[R_{L} = \frac{R_{0}}{\text{VSWR}}\] \[R_{L} = \frac{75}{3} = 25\,\Omega\] Since the load resistance can be either \(25\,\Omega\) or \(225\,\Omega\), the statement that it can only be \(25\,\Omega\) is false. \[\boxed{(B):False}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A load impedance, \((200 + j0)\ \Omega\) is to be matched to a \(50\ \Omega\) lossless transmission line by using a quarter wave line transformer (QWT). The characteristic impedance of the QWT required is ________.
questions.explanation: For a quarter-wave (\(\lambda/4\)) transformer, the characteristic impedance (\(Z_{0}\)) is related to the input impedance (\(Z_{in}\)) and the load impedance (\(Z_{L}\)) by the formula: \[Z_{0}^{2} = Z_{in} \cdot Z_{L}\] Given: \[Z_{in} = 50\,\Omega\] \[Z_{L} = 200\,\Omega\] Substituting these values into the expression: \[Z_{0}^{2} = 50 \times 200\] \[Z_{0}^{2} = 10000\] Taking the square root to find \(Z_{0}\): \[Z_{0} = \sqrt{10000}\] \[Z_{0} = 100\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{100}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The interior of a \(\dfrac{20}{3}\text{ cm} \times \dfrac{20}{4}\text{ cm}\) rectangular waveguide is completely filled with a dielectric of \(\epsilon_r = 4\). Waves of free space wave lengths shorter than _____ can be propagated in the \(\text{TE}_{11}\) mode.
questions.explanation: First, calculate the phase velocity (\(v\)) of the wave in the medium with dielectric constant \(\epsilon_{r} = 4\): \[v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0}\epsilon_{0}\epsilon_{r}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0}\epsilon_{0}}} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r}}}\] Given the speed of light in free space \(c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0}\epsilon_{0}}} = 3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}\): \[v = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{\sqrt{4}} = 1.5 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}\] For the mode \(m = n = 1\), the cut-off frequency (\(f_{c}\)) formula is: \[f_{c} = \frac{v}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{a}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{n}{b}\right)^{2}}\] Using \(a = 20\,\text{cm} = 0.2\,\text{m}\) and \(b = 15\,\text{cm} = 0.15\,\text{m}\) (implied from the calculation): \[f_{c} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{8}}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{0.2}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{1}{0.15}\right)^{2}}\] \[f_{c} = 0.75 \times 10^{8} \sqrt{5^{2} + 6.67^{2}} \approx 1.875 \times 10^{9}\,\text{Hz} = 1.875\,\text{GHz}\] Finally, determine the cut-off wavelength (\(\lambda_{c}\)): \[\lambda_{c} = \frac{v}{f_{c}} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{8}}{1.875 \times 10^{9}} = 0.08\,\text{m} = 8\,\text{cm}\] \[\boxed{8\,\text{cm}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: For a half-wave dipole antenna, which of the following statements are right?
options: The radiation intensity is maximum along the normal to the dipole axis.
The current distribution along its length is uniform irrespective of the length.
The effective length equals its physical length.
The input impedance is independent of the location of the feed point.
questions.explanation:
The radiation characteristics of a dipole antenna depend significantly on its length relative to the operating wavelength \(\lambda\). For a finite-length dipole, the far-field radiation pattern is given by: \[E(\theta) \propto \frac{\cos\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \cos \theta \right)}{\sin \theta}\] where \(\theta\) is the angle measured from the dipole axis. The pattern reaches its maximum at \(\theta = 90^\circ\) (perpendicular to the axis). The current distribution along the antenna is generally non-uniform, except for very short antennas like the Hertzian dipole. For a half-wave (\(\lambda/2\)) dipole, the effective length \(l_{\text{eff}}\) is defined as: \[l_{\text{eff}} = \frac{2l}{\pi}\] where \(l\) is the physical length of the antenna. The input impedance \(Z_{\text{in}}\) of a wire antenna is not constant; it is strongly influenced by the loading effects from the geometry and the distribution of current on either side of the feed point. \[\boxed{(A):\text{The radiation intensity is maximum along the normal to the dipole axis}}\]
Key points
  • Radiation Pattern: The \(\frac{\cos(\frac{\pi}{2} \cos \theta)}{\sin \theta}\) term describes the pattern of a resonant half-wave dipole.
